before.approach: The X Couloir is approached from the south via the Middle Fork Nooksack River Road (FR-38), not from Heliotrope Ridge (that trailhead serves Lincoln's separate NW Face/Wilkes-Booth line). Drive FR-38 toward its mile-12.5 switchback and start hiking/bushwhacking the old decommissioned road around Pt. 4481 toward Rankin Creek — snow travel (often by bike or snowshoe on the lower stretch) leads past East Rankin Lake (~5,120 ft) and up into the basin to a sheltered camp at treeline around 6,100 ft, near the highest trees in the basin below Seward Peak. From camp, an alpine start gets the team into the southwest basin and across the bergschrund crux while it's still cold and firm, climbing roughly 1,500 ft of 30-40° snow and a steep serac step in the X Couloir to the 9,085 ft summit. Total approach is on the order of 7 miles and 3,350 ft of gain to the basin camp. IMPORTANT — access note: as of mid-2026, FR-38 (Middle Fork Nooksack River Road) has reported washout damage from the December 2025 flood season with no confirmed repair timeline, and a separate seasonal gate at Wallace Creek (~mile 10) closes the road December 1-June 15 for elk calving; confirm current road status with the Mount Baker Ranger District (Glacier Public Service Center) before a trip, since the drivable road-end — and therefore the length of the approach — varies year to year.

approach_variants.name: Middle Fork Nooksack Road (FR-38) and Rankin Creek to the treeline camp, then the southwest basin
approach_variants.notes:
IMPORTANT AND FIRST: the X Couloir is approached from the SOUTH via the Middle Fork Nooksack River Road (FR-38), not from Heliotrope Ridge. Heliotrope serves Lincoln's separate northwest-face line. Getting this wrong puts you on the opposite side of the mountain with a glacier between you and your route.

Drive FR-38 toward its mile-12.5 switchback and start walking the old decommissioned road around Point 4481 toward Rankin Creek. Snow travel — often by bike or snowshoe on the lower stretch — leads past East Rankin Lake near 5,120 ft and up into the basin to a sheltered camp at treeline around 6,100 ft, by the highest trees in the basin below Seward Peak. Roughly seven miles and 3,350 ft of gain to camp.

ACCESS: as of mid-2026 FR-38 has reported washout damage from the December 2025 floods with no confirmed repair timeline, and a separate gate at Wallace Creek near mile 10 closes the road 1 December to 15 June for elk calving. Confirm the drivable road-end with the Mount Baker Ranger District before the trip; the length of the approach varies year to year.
approach_variants.season: Roughly May-Jul. A spring snow climb; essentially never done in summer, because what makes it climbable is continuous snow rather than the rubble underneath
hazards: A bergschrund crossing that must be done cold and early
1,500 ft of 30-40 degree snow with a steep serac step, all of it above a long runout
FR-38 flood damage with no repair timeline, plus an elk-calving gate closed 1 Dec - 15 Jun
A gully that funnels rockfall and spindrift after storms
A descent that is a real rappel sequence off pickets and slung horns, not a walk-off
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE HIGHEST TREES IN THE BASIN ARE THE CAMP, AND THE CAMP IS THE LAST THING YOU CAN NAVIGATE TO. Above treeline the southwest side of Lincoln is open snow and there is nothing to hold on to in cloud. So the arrival marker is vegetative rather than topographic: climb until the trees stop, and camp at the last of them, below Seward Peak, around 6,100 ft.

THE BERGSCHRUND IS THE BASE OF THE CLIMB. From camp an alpine start takes you into the southwest basin and to the schrund while the snow is still cold and firm. Above it is roughly 1,500 ft of 30-40 degree snow with a steep serac step in it.

DO NOT EXPECT ONE CLEAN COULOIR — THIS IS THE TRAP THE NAME SETS. Parties who have climbed and skied it describe it as less a couloir and more a series of steep chutes and faces, and the line drops from the high point to the highest notch, then down a narrow chute, and trends right out of view. So 'find the obvious couloir' is the wrong instruction and will have you standing in the basin looking for something that is not there. Work from the notch downward: the correct line is the one that connects to the HIGHEST notch on the skyline, and it is narrow where it leaves the basin.

THE SERAC STEP IS THE CONFIRMATION. Somewhere in that 1,500 ft you meet a steep serac step. A line with no ice step in it is not the X Couloir.

AND THE ASPECT SETTLES THE COARSE ERROR: this route faces SOUTHWEST and you reach it from Rankin Creek. If you are standing on the Coleman Glacier looking at a shaded north-facing cirque, you have come in from Heliotrope and you are under the other route on this mountain.

before.season: May-Jul (spring snow climb; essentially never done in summer)

before.approach: Same trailhead and lower approach as the standard line: start at the Heliotrope Ridge Trailhead (FS Road 39, Trail #677) near Glacier, WA, and follow the Heliotrope Ridge Trail roughly 2.7-3 miles through old-growth forest and several avalanche-chute creek crossings to the flat former Kulshan Cabin site (~3,200 ft), the usual camp/staging area. From there, climb the Hogsback moraine to the toe of the Coleman Glacier and rope up for glacier travel — but where the standard route cuts southwest toward the Thunder Glacier cirque, the north ridge/north-face approach stays higher and further climber's-right (east) on the Coleman Glacier, traversing beneath the Coleman icefall to reach the north-facing cirque wedged between Colfax Peak and Lincoln Peak. This is a longer, more exposed glacier traverse than the standard approach: you pass directly beneath active serac bands on the Coleman Glacier's upper icefall for a stretch, so icefall/serac collapse is a real objective hazard here and timing (early morning, before the glacier softens) matters more than on the SW-side approach. The line aims for the base of Lincoln's roughly 1,000-ft north face/ridge, a route first climbed in May 1958 (Cooper and O'Conner) that 'demanded ice screws' — meaning it's genuinely an ice/mixed objective, not a snow scramble, and conditions (rime, verglas, bare ice) vary a lot by season and year; go early-season (spring) for the best ice, which also generally means better-bridged crevasses on the glacier crossing.

approach_variants.name: Heliotrope Ridge to the Kulshan Cabin site, then high and right on the Coleman beneath the icefall
approach_variants.notes: Start at the Heliotrope Ridge Trailhead on FS Road 39, Trail #677, near Glacier. Follow the trail roughly 2.7-3 miles through old growth and several avalanche-chute creek crossings to the flat former Kulshan Cabin site around 3,200 ft, which is the usual camp and staging area. From there climb the Hogsback moraine to the toe of the Coleman Glacier and rope up. Where the party heading for the southwest side of the mountain would cut away toward the Thunder Glacier cirque, this route stays HIGHER and further climber's RIGHT — east — on the Coleman, traversing beneath the Coleman icefall to reach the north-facing cirque wedged between Colfax Peak and Lincoln Peak. That traverse is longer and more exposed than the south-side approach: for a stretch you are directly beneath active serac bands on the upper icefall, so serac collapse is a real objective hazard and an early, cold start matters more here than it does on the other side of the mountain. NOTE ON THIS ROUTE: it names one first-ascent party in its first-ascent record and a different, much earlier one in its approach prose. Treat the route's history as unsettled; the ground described is not in doubt.
approach_variants.season: Winter to early spring. The only documented ascent was mid-March, in a lean cold winter — this is an ice objective and it needs the ice to exist
hazards: Traversing directly beneath active serac bands on the Coleman icefall
Crevasses on a long, exposed, high traverse of the Coleman
Roughly 1,000 ft of ice and mixed ground with conditions that vary enormously year to year
Loose rock reported on the face, which matters because the descent means building anchors on it
No documented independent descent — parties either reverse the face or traverse to the southwest gully
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BASE IS A CIRQUE WITH A PEAK ON EACH SIDE OF IT, AND THAT IS THE TEST. Lincoln's north face sits in a north-facing cirque WEDGED BETWEEN COLFAX PEAK AND LINCOLN PEAK. You have arrived when the ground you are standing on is enclosed on two sides by rock rising to two separate summits, with the Coleman behind you. One peak above you is not enough; you need the cirque.

THE HANDRAIL IS THE ICEFALL, AND IT IS OVERHEAD RATHER THAN UNDERFOOT. From the Coleman's toe, stay HIGH and go RIGHT, traversing beneath the icefall. Icefall above you on your left is the confirmation you are on the correct traverse; it is also the reason to be there before the sun. If you find yourself descending toward a cirque with no icefall above you, you have cut left toward the Thunder Glacier side and are heading for the southwest face.

THE FACE ITSELF IS ABOUT 1,000 FT AND IT IS ICE. If the wall in front of you is a snow slope you could walk, it is not this route. The historical record for this line is explicit that it demanded ice screws, and modern accounts grade it WI4/AI4+; rime, verglas and bare ice vary hugely by year, so what you find may be harder or easier than the grade but it will not be a scramble.

GO EARLY IN THE SEASON FOR TWO REASONS AT ONCE: the ice is better, and the crevasses on the traverse are better bridged. Those two arguments point the same way, which is unusual and worth using.

WHAT BEING ON THE WRONG SIDE LOOKS LIKE: open snow basin, sun on your back, trees below you at 6,100 ft. That is the X Couloir approach from Rankin Creek and it is reached from a different road entirely.

partner_requirements.approachTime: Long glacier approach below the Black Buttes before the technical ridge climbing begins; plan an alpine start well before dawn
requiredSkills: Confident movement on loose Class 4-low 5th rock
Route-finding on serious terrain with unreliable anchors

before.descent_text: There is no walk-off from the top of the north ridge/north face — it's a rappelling descent back down steep, often loose terrain. Because the north face has no established independent descent line, parties either reverse the ridge/face itself or (more commonly, per the pattern typical of routes like this) traverse over on the upper mountain to descend the easier, well-traveled southwest gully (the 'X Couloir' used as the standard route's descent) rather than rappel the full north face a second time. Reversing the route means building rappel anchors off slung rock horns and blocks through the steepest ice and mixed sections — the rock here is loose, so test anchors and blocks carefully and avoid pulling ropes across bare rock edges. Given the face is roughly 1,000 ft (~300m) of sustained steep ground, and using a single rope doubled (~30m per rappel) is the standard setup for anchors of this type, expect on the order of 4-6 rappels through the steepest ice/mixed sections with some downclimbing or simul-climbing on the more moderate snow between them if descending the face directly; if instead you traverse to the standard SW gully, expect a rappel sequence similar to that route's (commonly up to 10 double-rope rappels off a mix of pickets and existing horn slings, conditions-dependent). Either way, re-rope once back on the Coleman Glacier for the crevassed descent back to the Hogsback moraine and the Heliotrope Ridge Trail.
before.watch_out:
Loose rock and lichen-covered sections throughout
Complex terrain with multiple approach/descent route options
Glacier travel hazards (Sherpa, Stuart glaciers) particularly late season
Water availability limited at notch (8,200 ft) depending on snowmelt
Navigation complexity - route-finding can be challenging
Weather exposure on open alpine terrain
Significant elevation gain over long day commitment
